newsitem.title: UK: Marches and guerrillas test N.Irish peace quest.
newsitem.headline: Marches and guerrillas test N.Irish peace quest.

text.p: Fears intensified in Northern Ireland on Sunday that a contentious pro-British parade might spill over into serious violence and blight struggling efforts to end a long war by Irish guerrillas fighting rule from London.

Secretary of State Mo Mowlam, desperate to defuse anxiety about a volatile Protestant "marching season" edging towards confrontation, gave a blunt warning that the region could not afford a repeat of chaos that flared last year.
"Some people seem determined to push Northern Ireland to the brink," she wrote in Belfast's Sunday Life newspaper. "We will all pay a very heavy price if they are allowed to succeed."

As worries grew that the most hotly disputed Protestant march - on July 6 at Drumcree - might trigger Protestant and Catholic clashes, outlawed IRA guerrillas were reported to have virtually ruled out any prospect of a truce before the series of pro-British marches end in August.
"I think people are feeling doom and gloom', and forebodings of the worst," Henry Patterson, a professor of law at the University of Ulster in Belfast, told Reuters.

Paul Bew, law lecturer at Queen's University, Belfast, said the community mood was tremulous and fearful, not just about the July 6 parade at Drumcree - the most hotly disputed of the marching season - but about the overall political situation.
"It is not just in relation to Drumcree, but also a fear that the peace process itself is going to die in some absolute sense over the next three months," Bew told Reuters.

All sides say that the air of pessimism, and a lingering uncertainty about whether the Irish Republican Army will grasp recent British peace initiatives, will not lift until the tension-laden marching season passes.

Moderate nationalists say that a package launched by British Prime Minister Tony Blair last week - holding out the prospect of a political settlement within a year and a talks seat for the IRA's political arm Sinn Fein six weeks after the guerrillas end a war on British rule - is a "last chance saloon" for the republican hardmen.
"It's time to fish or cut bait, as they politely say in the States," chimed a Catholic nationalist who was unwilling to speculate on the chances of the IRA embracing the new deal.

Divisions have emerged between the province's Protestant parties, who speak for the pro-British majority population, about when guerrillas should surrender arms, and that could have a crucial bearing on the republican attitude the peace package.
Many in both camps are sceptical that the guerrillas, who style themselves defenders of beleagured Catholics, will scrap guns before a final settlement is secured.

Britain and Ireland want the IRA, once it ends violence, to discard arms at the same time as talks progress on an agenda that would allow Sinn Fein to argue for their joint goal of unifying Northern Ireland with the Irish Republic.
Drumcree Catholics, who oppose British rule, say the march by the Orange Order brotherhood is intimidating and anti-Irish.
They accuse Britain of buckling under Protestant pressure by allowing the Orangemen through their zone last year.
Orangemen assert that nationalists fired by anti-British feeling are trying to disrupt the parade, which they say is a simple display of pride in their religious faith.
Clashes swept the region last July when police reversed a four-day ban on the march after Protestant street violence.

Trouble has flared at Drumcree for two successive years. Security chiefs are bracing themselves for more outbreaks. Analysts say trouble will harden political attitudes. "Events on the ground have a way of taking over," said Patterson.
Bew felt that if the parade is not allowed down the disputed Catholic Garvaghy Road, there will be a bitter reaction by Orange supporters.
"But it will not be on the scale of last year, because it is clear that sections of the Orange leadership feel that displays of violence and extremism actually play into the IRA's hands.
"If it goes down, I suppose the projected Blair honeymoon with the Republican movement (IRA and Sinn Fein) is off."
